entries.text: The Domesday Book recorded a mill on the River Soar, its rental value of 6s 8d (about 33p). This mill had been providing basic mechanical power for grinding the local corn before this date
Norman overlords added two churches, St John's Chapel in the North, St Michael & All Angels in the South.
A windmill was in existence
St. John's Chapel falls into disrepair
Grange Farm is in existance on Sugar Lane (now Bridge Park Road)
The Enclosures Act
Roman milestone was discovered
Founding of the Wesleyan Chapel (Rebuilt in 1886)
Leicester section of the Soar Navigation Canal opened and Thurmaston was provided with a lock
North and South Thurmaston became a combined chapelry
The Boat Inn, beside Thurmaston’s coal wharf at the end of Boatyard Lane (now Wharf Street) was in business to serve the canal traffic.
A will of 1811 reveals the earliest known tenant of the Black Horse (William Smith of Sileby)
drummer William Lane was killed in Thurmaston in 1822
The White Hart is used as a Coroner's Court for the inquest of William Lane, the soldier murdered by John Bishop Allen
A public house, possibly named The Wellington was in existence. (Later to become The Harrow.)
The Harrow is noted.
The original Vicarage was built (replaced in 1975)
Population 1229 (950 of the manufacturing class)
census shows the Gibbins family, owners of the watermill living on the corner of Mill Lane, in a property that also doubled as a shop and bakery.
Thurmaston becomes a separate Ecclesiastical Parish, with St. Michael's becoming the parish church.
National School built
Fence added to front of the National School Thos. Allen became Squire of the South Manor (whose house was the Manor)
St. Michael’s Church restored and enlarged with tower estored, new clock, extra bell and Holditch Barrel organ and the churchyard extended and enclosed on three sides by granite walling.
Havelock Cottages and hosiery factory built on Garden Street
The School House was built
Board floor built above concrete floor on National School
January Fletcher Bail opened up a Post Office within his grocery shop close to St Michael’s Church
occupants of Thurmaston Hall are listed as the Sheriffe family
Dudley Row built
The Generous Briton began life as a beer house on Pingle Road or Close (now Garden Street)
National School extended
Glebe Farmhouse,(formerley called 'The Retreat') which stands on Wharf Street between Forest Avenue and Unicorn Street was built
Ellmore's was in production
Population 1545
Primitive Methodist Chapel built (Parkers)
Leicester brick manufacturers Messrs Henry Herbert and Sons of 33 Millstone Lane took over Thurmaston’s Star Brick Works situated by the Midland Railway line on Humberstone Lane
William Preston was Postmaster in his bakery shop in premesis now known as 'Papilion' 723 Melton Rd
Wesleyan Chapel built (next to Conservative Club)
Rose Terrace (Melton Road shops) is built
School fees abolished
‘The great frost' January and February 1895 picture of skaters on frozen River Soar
Melrose Villas built (Canal Street, right side going towards river.
terraced Maryville Row built (opposite The Harrow Inn)
Pot Row Villas, (Westview (Rogers, Fairfield News) Newark Villas
Terraced houses and shops are built on junction of Herricks Avenue (now Humberstone Lane) and Melton Road
A Liberal Club in the former Methodist Chapel building in Garden Street is first listed in a directory. (forerunner to Thurmaston working Mens' Club)
National School extended
Civil parish of Thurmaston formed
Belmont Villas built (opposite Conservative Club) Weymouth Villas built (opposite Conservative Club) Scarisbrook Villas built (opposite Conservative Club)
Holly Houses (Humberstone Lane (Wing Sun & Bookmakers) Ivy Houses (Cybershop)
The True Blue which closed (bottom of Mill Lane).
The factory for Peptine Maltine Ltd was built on land from the bottom of Wharf Street to what is now Unicorn Street and right down to the Canal.
The Post Office had transferred to a draper’s shop, Borderick tailors between the Black Horse and the Wesleyan Chapel.
First World War
400 troops billeted in the National School
Telephone arrived in the village

The Liberal Club is provided with a modern image together with a move to a large new club building near the corner of Cemetery Road (now Hadrian Road) and is renamed ‘Thurmaston Working Men’s Club and Institute’.
A house and shop onthe corner of Mill Lane was bought by Frederick Cockbill and became the Post Office.
Thurmaston’s very first village telephone in the Post Office
December 8th, Joe Bradshaw became the first person to be killed by a motor car in Thurmaston.
Malt Factory at the bottom of Canal Street burned down
Thurmaston Bethel Methodist Chapel (stone laid by Geo. E. Hilton esq.) Whit Monday May 28th
Herbert and Sons formed the Highway Sand and Gravel Pits in Thurmaston (closed in the 1940s)

local entrepreneur, Walter Nokes had bought the empty water mill with its three islands on the River and turned the site into a Pleasure Garden. A cafe, together with tennis, clock golf, croquet, putting green, paddleboats, rowing boats and punts provided entertainment, with the millwheels powering a generator for coloured lights around the grounds.
Feb 23rd. Mrs Agnes Checkland, of Thurmaston Hall, on Humberstone Lane, laid the foundation stone of the Memorial Hall on February.
Thurmaston War Memorial Hall built by En-tout-Cas
April 9th Roundhill Modern School opened (officially opened on July 9th)
Revd Botterill came to Thurmaston
Mill demolished c.1930
The Peptine Maltine factory was destroyed by fire in August

Frederick Cockbill established the Post Office in what was previously a private house next to his grocer’s shop. He had bought the premises, situated on the corner of Mill Lane and Main Street, four years earlier from Thomas Gibbins, who had been Thurmaston’s miller and baker.
The present Scout group was formed with Thomas Moore as Scoutmaster and the Revd Botterill as Group Scoutmaster. They met in the vicar's stables in the Vicarage grounds.

The Scout Band was initially formed with a bugle (from a pawnbrokers shop in Jersey) and a side drum. The first outing was a church parade followed by Silver Jubilee celebrations for George V when the band played at a street party in the village.
The Scout troop numbers reached 150 scouts and Phil Taylor and Syd Taylor joined the group and started a cub pack
A fire, destroying a nearby car spread to the old watermill which was demolished shortly after
The final landlord of the Black Horse, George Smith, took the license to the new Manor Hotel in 1938
Taylorcraft Aeroplanes (England) Limited was registered as a private company to make and sell aircraft for the British Empire and Europe.
Black Horse demolished
Construction started in February 1939 in rented premises behind Crowthers at Britannia Works for premises to build aircraft by Taylorcraft Aeroplanes (England) Limited
1st September beginning of WW2
Site of the Black Horse used as air raid shelter
2nd September 1945 end of WW2
DCE and Weetabix moved to Thurmaston 1940s (late)The Roundway, formerly Roundway Road (unadopted) is resurfaced by the residents
The Roundway is adopted after widening to conform to regulations
work begins on 'The Dales' estate
Five Infant classrooms built on Church Hill Road School
Church Hill Road Infants School (Thurmaston Infant School) opens
Main Street renamed as Melton Road
Factory built on Humberstone Lane for Dallow Lambert & Co Ltd, and traded as engineers and sheet metal workers. (to be named DCE in 1963)
January - work began on the construction of Thurmaston 'by-pass'
August A pedestrian subway was constructed to join Brook Street and Churchill Road under the by-pass
Grange Farm is sold and becomes a car showroom
A sub-Post Office moved from Humberstone Lane and established it in his grocery business on The Dales Estate, Lonsdale Road naming it Checklands Post Office
saw the development of a Youth Wing, a swimming pool and evening classes which marked the change from Roundhill Modern School to a High School and later a Community College
October, By-pass opened to traffic
Church Hill Road Junior School opened

Dallow Lambert Limited on Humberstone Lane was sold to the Thomas Tilling Group and the name changed to Dust Control Equipment Ltd. (DCE). A research and development block was opened on the Thurmaston site. (See 2000)
Traffic lights installed at junction of Humberstone Lane and the by-pass
National School no longer used as a school - became Teacher Centre and Leics. Resource Centre.
28th Feb Eastfield School opened
Wesleyan Chapel becomes commercial premises
The brick arch of Johnsons Bridge was removed and replaced by a concrete structure.
Church Hill Road surfaced.
Houses in 'New Thurmaston', Reading Street & Berkeley Street are demolished
Offranville flats built on Silverdale Drive
New Vicarage built and old one is demolished to be replaced by Estelle House
a small group of pupils from Roundhill College carried out an excavation of the old St. John's Chapel ruins
A Co-op is mentioned on Main Street (now 729 Melton Road)
February, the Old Hall on Canal Street is demolished to make way for Old Hall Close
Havelock cottages demolished

Thurmaston Bowls Club first met on February 20th. 18 members decided to form a club for both ladies and gentlemen so they would play in mixed matches. At Elizabeth Park there was a wooden pavilion situated next to the bowling green
The White Hart is renamed 'The Taverna'
February, Britannia Tower is demolished
Final service held at the Primitave Methodist Chapel
Michael Westwood Stationery established (later became Thurmaston Print Shop)
The excavation of gravel began forming the lakes which are now part of Watermead Country Park.
March/April First issue of the Thurmaston Times
Street Fayre to raise funds for St Michael's roof
Sat 24th 1pm August Elizabeth Park opened by THE LORD LIEUTENANT OF LEICESTERSHIRE
Elizabeth Park Sports & Community Centre was officially opened on 24th August
Fundraising for a new roof at St. Michael's Churh raised £32,000.
After a number of name changes DCE is acquired by an American filtration company the Donaldson Group
Sunny Textiles burnt down in 2003 (site of Black Horse)
17th July, Post Office closes at the corner of Mill Lane. The only other PO in Thurmaston is now on Lonsdale Road, over the 'by-pass'
Thurmaston Heritage Group formed
A statue was unveiled in on Garden Street in memory of the drummer William Lane who was killed in Thurmaston in 1822
after a break of eight years Thurmaston Carnival was restarted with the theme of the day 'Thurmaston by the Sea’, with donkey rides, sandpits, buckets and spades.
Thurmaston Bowls Club celebrated it’s 25thAnniversary
The Etchells Signs factory on Garden Street was demolished to make way for housing (Havelock Gardens)
Memories Of Thurmaston (1) is published by Thurmaston Heritage Group
Speed limit on Newark Road 'by-pass' was reduced from 70mph to 50mph
Memories Of Thurmaston (2) is published by Thurmaston Heritage Group
Major fire at Thurmaston Shopping Centre
New Prime Minister
